SYSTEM DESIGN SERIES | 02
Consistency, 
Durability & 
Availability
What your data promises, and what  
it costs
Part 2 · follows Part 1: Tail Latency

THE THREE PROMISES
What does saving data really promise?
C
Consistency
Do all readers see the same,  
latest data?
D
Durability
Once saved, will the data still  
exist later?
A
Availability
Can I read and write right now?
Each promise has a cost. Let’s put numbers on them.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 02

AVAILABILITY
Counting the nines
Downtime = (1 − availability) × time. Example: (1 − 0.999) × 8,760 hours = 8.76 hours
Availability Downtime per year Per month (30 days)
99% 3.65 days (87.6 hours) 7.2 hours
99.9% 8.76 hours 43.2 minutes
99.99% 52.6 minutes 4.32 minutes
99.999% 5.26 minutes 25.9 seconds
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 03

DEPENDENCIES IN SERIES
99.5%
availability of the whole request
Five services, each 99.9% available, and the  
request needs all five.
0.999⁵ ≈ 99.50%
Downtime: (1 − 0.99501) × 8,760 hours ≈ 43.7 hours a year, compared with 8.76 hours for a single  
99.9% service.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 04

REDUNDANCY IN PARALLEL
Redundant copies raise availability
Availability = 1 − (1 − A)ⁿ, with A = 99% per copy
1 copy
99%
1 − 0.01 = 0.99
87.6 hours of downtime a year
2 copies
99.99%
1 − 0.01² = 0.9999
52.6 minutes a year
3 copies
99.9999%
1 − 0.01³ = 0.999999
about 31.5 seconds a year
This assumes failures are independent. A shared rack, region or bad deploy can take down all copies at once.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 05

DURABILITY
Will the data still exist later?
1 · ONE COPY
P(lost) = 1% 
= 0.01
Assume each copy has a 1%  
chance of being lost in a year.
2 · ALL 3 LOST
0.01 × 0.01 × 0.01 
= 0.000001
Losses are independent, so the  
probabilities multiply.
3 · DURABILITY
1 − 0.000001 
= 99.9999%
Data survives unless every copy  
is lost.
Durability is not availability: durable data can still be unreachable right now. This assumes independent failures and no repair.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 06

DURABILITY AT SCALE
Why nines matter with 10 million objects
Expected losses a year = objects × (1 − durability)
6 NINES · 99.9999%
1 − 0.999999 = 0.000001 
10,000,000 × 0.000001 = 10
≈10 objects lost a year
11 NINES · 99.999999999%
1 − 0.99999999999 = 0.00000000001 
10,000,000 × 0.00000000001 = 0.0001 
1 ÷ 0.0001 = 10,000 years
about one object per 10,000 years
More objects means more chances that one is lost, so small differences in durability matter at scale. This assumes  
independent failures.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 07

CONSISTENCY
What is a read allowed to see?
Strong consistency
Every read returns the latest acknowledged write.
Trade-off: replicas must coordinate, which adds latency  
and can reduce availability during failures.
Eventual consistency
Replicas converge over time. A read may briefly  
return older data.
Trade-off: faster and more available, but readers can see  
stale data for a moment.
Example: you change your profile photo, then refresh. With eventual consistency you may briefly see the old one.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 08

QUORUMS
Quorums: R + W > N
N = replicas, W = write acknowledgements, R = replicas read. Here N = 3.
Setup R + W Reads see the latest write?
W = 3, R = 1 4 > 3 Yes
W = 2, R = 2 4 > 3 Yes
W = 1, R = 3 4 > 3 Yes
W = 1, R = 1 2 ≤ 3 No, reads may be stale
When R + W > N, every read consults at least one replica that holds the latest acknowledged write.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 09

READ-WRITE RATIO
10,000 requests a second at 95 : 5
Reads 9,500 / s
Writes 500 / s
10,000 × 0.95 = 9,500 reads/s · 10,000 × 0.05 = 500 writes/s
Ratio = 9,500 : 500 = 19 : 1. Reads dominate.
Replica work = reads × R + writes × N
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 10

THE TRADE-OFF
W and R for a 95 : 5 workload
N = 3 replicas, each node 99.9% available. All three settings keep R + W > N.
Setup Replica ops/s Read availability Write availability
W=3, R=1 11,000 99.9999999% 99.70%
W=2, R=2 20,500 99.9997% 99.9997%
W=1, R=3 30,000 99.70% 99.9999999%
W=3, R=1: 500 × 3 + 9,500 × 1 = 11,000 ops/s. A write needs 3 of 3 nodes up: 0.999³ = 99.70%.
W=3, R=1 is cheapest for a read-heavy load, but one node down blocks writes: about 26 hours a year. W=2, R=2 costs about 1.9× the  
work and loses about 1.6 minutes a year.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 11

KEY TAKEAWAY
Consistency, durability and availability are not free. 
Every nine, every replica and every quorum setting is a  
trade, and the read-write ratio shows which side to  
make cheap.
These calculations assume independent failures. Real systems also face correlated failures and network partitions.
System Design Series | 02 · Consistency, Durability & Availability 12

OVER TO YOU
Which trade-off have you had to make  
in production?
Consistency Availability Durability
Which one did you give up first, and why? This is Part 2 of my System Design series. Part 1 was Tail Latency.
